title: Explaining it
hookLine: scholars explain verses by other verses, hadith, language and context

lines: WHICH OF US HAS NEVER DONE WRONG?
THEY TOOK IT TO THE PROPHET.
cards: A verse says that those who believe, and don't mix their belief with wrongdoing, are the ones who will be safe. When the companions heard it, they were frightened. Which of us, they asked, has never done wrong?
If that's the condition, who is safe? They took the question straight to the Prophet ﷺ. His answer didn't come out of nowhere.
He pointed them to another verse.

teach.b: The Prophet told them: it isn't what you think. Haven't you heard what Luqman said to his son? And he recited from Surah 31, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! to ascribe partners (unto Him) is a tremendous wrong."

The wrong meant in the first verse was that one: setting up partners with God, not every everyday failing. The companions could breathe again. That story, in Bukhari, is the seed of tafsir, explaining the Qur'an.
The word comes from a root meaning to uncover, to lay open. Scholars have climbed the same ladder ever since.
First, the Qur'an explains the Qur'an: one verse opens another, as Luqman's line opened the first.

Second, the Prophet's words and example, the hadith. Third, the understanding of the companions who were there, like Ibn Abbas, for whom the Prophet prayed that he be given understanding of the religion.

Fourth, the Arabic language itself: grammar, rare words, even old Arabic poetry, which Ibn Abbas is reported to have used to explain unusual words. And context: the occasions of revelation you met eleven days ago.
From these came the great written commentaries.
Al-Tabari, in the tenth century, gathered the early reports verse by verse into a huge work. Ibn Kathir, in the fourteenth, wrote what is still one of the most read commentaries.

Others focus on law, or language, or the inner meanings the Sufis looked for. And scholars warn against explaining the Qur'an by personal opinion alone, without knowledge. Tafsir isn't a way of adding to the book.
It's a way of listening to it more closely, letting its own verses, and the people nearest to it, speak first.

how: Muslims read tafsir, commentary on the Qur'an, in study circles, in Friday sermons and at home; classic commentaries like those of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir are widely read and translated.

games.q: you're a companion. a verse says only those who don't mix belief with wrongdoing are safe. what do you do?
o: ask the Prophet what it means.
games.why: they asked, and he explained it by another verse: the wrong meant was ascribing partners to God, not every failing.

practice: Hold one verse you know, maybe the opening of al-Ikhlas, that God is One, and ask: where else in the Qur'an have I heard this idea? Let another verse come to mind, or just let the question sit.

wordCard.voice: Tafsir. Explaining the Qur'an, from a root meaning to uncover: by the Qur'an itself, the hadith, the companions and the language. Today's word.
